Plain-Language Contract Summary

Section 7 — Indemnification & Limitation of Liability

Who covers whom when something goes wrong, and how much money is on the line.

The task: Summarize Section 7 of the contract for a non-lawyer, and translate the key legal terms into plain English.

The Short Version

Section 7 does two related things. First, it says that if a third party sues one of the parties because of something the other party did (like breaking a promise in the contract, being seriously careless, or shipping something that infringes someone's patent or copyright), the party at fault has to step in, take over the lawsuit, and pay the bill.

Second, it puts a hard ceiling on the kinds of damages and the total dollar amount either party can be forced to pay under this contract — with a few important exceptions that break through that ceiling.

7.1 — Who Pays When Someone Else Sues

Each party promises to protect the other from third-party lawsuits that arise from three specific things:

  1. Broken promises — a party breaks a representation, warranty, or covenant in the contract.
  2. Serious misconduct — a party is grossly negligent or intentionally does something wrong.
  3. IP infringement — a party's Deliverables (the work product it hands over) allegedly infringe someone else's intellectual property.

The IP promise has three carve-outs. The infringing party does not owe protection if the problem was caused by:

  • The other side modifying the Deliverables,
  • The other side combining the Deliverables with something else that caused the infringement, or
  • The other side using the Deliverables in a way the contract didn't allow.

7.2 — How the Process Works

If a covered lawsuit shows up, the party being sued must:

  • Give prompt written notice to the party that owes protection (though a late notice only hurts them if the delay actually caused real harm to the defense).
  • Hand over the driver's seat — let the indemnifying party run the defense and negotiate any settlement. But that party can't agree to a settlement that admits fault or forces the other side to do something (as opposed to just paying money) without written permission.
  • Cooperate reasonably, with expenses covered by the party running the defense.

7.3 — The Cap on Damages

This is written in all-caps in the original for a reason: it's the money-limiting clause. It has two parts.

Part A: No indirect damages

Neither party can sue the other for “soft” damages — things like lost profits, lost revenue, damaged reputation, or lost data — even if the other side was warned that those losses might happen.

Part B: A total dollar ceiling

The most either party can owe the other, in total, is the larger of:

  • The fees the Customer paid (or owes) in the 12 months before the problem started, or
  • $100,000.
Important: the cap has holes. Both the “no indirect damages” rule and the dollar cap do not apply to: (i) the indemnification obligations in 7.1, (ii) breaches of confidentiality (Section 9), (iii) gross negligence or willful misconduct, or (iv) infringing the other party's intellectual property. For any of those, a party can be on the hook for the full amount of the harm.

What This Means at a Glance

SituationIs there a $ cap?Are indirect damages allowed?
Ordinary contract disputeYes — greater of 12 months' fees or $100KNo
Indemnified third-party claim (7.1)No capYes (as awarded)
Confidentiality breachNo capYes
Gross negligence or willful misconductNo capYes
IP infringement of the other party's rightsNo capYes

Key Legal Terms in Plain Language

Indemnify
To promise, in advance, that you'll cover another party's losses if a specific kind of trouble happens — and usually to handle the fight yourself.
Defend, indemnify, and hold harmless
The full package: (1) show up and run the legal defense, (2) pay any damages or settlement, and (3) make sure the protected party ends up no worse off financially.
Indemnifying Party / Indemnified Party
The one making the promise to protect (Indemnifying) versus the one being protected (Indemnified).
Third-party claim
A lawsuit or demand brought by someone outside the contract — not by the other party themselves.
Representation, warranty, or covenant
Three kinds of contractual promises. A representation is a statement of fact; a warranty is a guarantee that something is or will be true; a covenant is a promise to do (or not do) something.
Gross negligence
Carelessness that goes well beyond an ordinary mistake — a reckless disregard for obvious risks.
Willful misconduct
Deliberately doing something wrong, or acting with knowledge that harm will likely result.
Infringe / misappropriate
Infringe means using someone's protected work (patent, copyright, trademark) without permission. Misappropriate usually refers to improperly taking or using a trade secret.
Deliverables
The tangible things one party hands over under the contract — software, documents, reports, designs, etc.
Tender sole control of the defense
Formally hand over the lawsuit — the party that owes indemnification picks the lawyers and calls the shots.
Materially prejudiced
Actually and significantly harmed — not just inconvenienced. Late notice only excuses the indemnifier if the delay caused real damage to the defense.
Not to be unreasonably withheld
A party has to say yes unless they have a genuinely good reason to say no; they can't refuse just to be difficult.
Indirect, incidental, consequential, special, punitive, or exemplary damages
Categories of damages that go beyond the immediate, direct loss. Examples: lost future profits, harm to reputation, or punishment-style awards. The clause blocks all of these.
Under any theory of liability
No matter what legal argument someone tries — contract, negligence, statute, etc. — the same limit applies.
Even if advised of the possibility of such damages
The cap holds even if the other party warned in advance that these losses could happen. Warning doesn't create liability.
Total cumulative liability
Everything added up together — not per claim, not per year. Once the cap is hit, it's hit for the life of the contract.
Fees paid or payable
Money already paid plus money owed but not yet paid. Both count toward the 12-month total used to calculate the cap.
This is a plain-language summary intended to aid understanding. It is not legal advice and does not replace the contract's actual language, which controls in any dispute.
